story_text.value:
I built an emulator of a flash-sale fashion outlet with no registration and fake checkout that never takes money. You can browse items that are on sale, watch in real time as they go out of stock one by one, and get notified when they are back on sale (possibly with different prices).
Every order placed on the website gets “tracking” which fails on the delivery day with one of 50 available reasons (for example, “a raccoon in the Newark depot has claimed your parcel; animal control reports that it seems happy there”). But you can also share the tracking with your friends, and they can hurry the courier; the more hurries, the more spectacularly it fails, until your parcel lands in the Svalbard seed vault, the North Pole, the International Space Station or some such place.
The complete shop contents (campaigns, prices, item availability and stock levels) are computed from the current time with a fixed seed (FNV-1a for hashing, mulberry32 as the PRNG). I wrote the mechanism first in JS and then ported to PHP (for the website) and Flutter (for the mobile app); a test ran over several thousand random time points to verify they are identical. The Flutter app uses its own generator because it can work offline - no contact with the website is necessary.
Item images are generated with OpenAI API, except models in swimsuits. OpenAI refused a lot of swimsuit image prompts, so I had to switch to Gemini for these as Gemini has no qualms about this kind of content.
Does this kind of site feel like shopping to you? Or more like a game or something to do together with friends?

title.value: Show HN: An online shop where your friends can hurry the courier

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I've built Rui (cotton in hindi), an agent runtime built for memory efficiency.

The main design choice is that sessions share a host rather than each being a process. Agents are state in DB and the host handles the active work through a share event loop.

LLMs are getting better at coordination and teams (swarms) of agents are coming. Memory is getting expensive and my machine is always using swap. We cannot be wasting hundreds of MBs of RAM for an orchestrator (AKA the harness) of LLMs and tools.

More information on the architecture and measurement methodology is at https://divyanshgolyan.com/posts/hundred-agents/

I'd love feedback about this design boxing me into a corner and any large tradeoffs I'm not seeing!

title.value: Show HN: Rui, orchestrating 100 agents in 2.5 MB of RAM

story_text.value:
Throughout this year I've been working on a game called Fermi Poker and have now published a guide on how to play and host a tournament. This guide includes a question set, a rule sheet to print out, and everything else you need to know. If you don't want to print out anything, you can also use fermi.org/play to see the questions on your device.

Fermi Poker combines the betting mechanics of poker with Fermi estimation questions like "How many new smartphones were sold worldwide in 2024?" or "How many chickens were slaughtered for meat worldwide in 2024?"

Once you've submitted a range estimate, there are four betting rounds, with two hints and the answer revealed between them.

The aspiration was to create a game that teaches important rationality concepts (Fermi estimation, Bayesian updating, cognitive empathy, world-modeling, emotional regulation, etc.)

If you want to host a tournament at your school or university, please consider reaching out as I can provide some funding to cover the cost of poker chips and small prizes.

title.value: Show HN: Fermi Poker, a combination of poker betting mechanics with estimation

story_text.value:
retex is a clean-room, CC0, reimplementation of LuaLaTeX in rust. It can either be used as a faster (x2-3) drop-in replacement for LuaLaTex (--compat mode) , or as a more modern TeX engine, with much nicer error messages, support for SVG, ODP/ODT output, native PDF/X1 and PDF/X4 for printing, auto-download of missing packages (like eg Miktex), python bindings, etc. User manual with examples: https://retex-ef747d.gitlab.io/retex-manual.pdf

retex has been entirely generated by a Large Language Model (LLM). Therefore, retex itself does not have any author. It is an automatic machine-translation of the work of D.E. Knuth and of the hundreds of volunteers who made TeX, LaTeX and LuaTeX what they are today. All credit goes to them.

title.value: Show HN: Retex, a Faster LaTeX Engine

story_text.value:
I built an automatic food-recall tracker that collects recalls from sources including the FDA, USDA, FSA, RASFF, and others. It currently covers the US, UK, Europe, Canada, and South Africa.

It uses ML to classify recalls by severity, cause, and category, and also tries to detect anomalies/outbreaks and identify similar recalls.

You can sign up for daily email alerts based on your preferences, so you can be notified when a recall is relevant to you (The emails are best-effort and shouldn't be treated as an authoritative source of safety information). My goal is simply to make it easier to keep track of recalls that might otherwise be missed.

I'd be particularly interested in feedback on the classification/anomaly detection, and other any other useful recall information could be added.

title.value: Show HN: I built a food recall tracker with ML classification and email alerts
